raw_response:
I have farmed this land since I was twenty years old. My mother farmed before me, and her mother before her. I do not need anyone to tell me what to do — I have seen forty-eight harvests on this soil. I know when to water by how the leaves curl. I know when the bollworm is coming before the extension workers do.

My land is 10.1 mu. Seven of those mu I rotate between winter wheat and summer maize — that is how we have always done it here in Quzhou. The remaining three mu I plant cotton. Cotton is hard work and my back is not what it was, but it brings cash, and I need cash more than grain. Some of my children have gone to work in the city. The ones who stay help during the busy weeks.

For wheat, I will plough in October, spread the base fertilizer, and sow. I will water before the ground freezes, water again at jointing, and again when the heads come out. I buy the improved seed from the village store — the hybrid corn too. I have used these for years. For the maize, I go in right after the wheat harvest in June. There is no time to waste. I use the rotary machine to turn the stubble and plant within a week. Maize only needs me to water if the July rains fail, which they sometimes do.

Cotton worries me most. Bollworm has been bad the last few years. I will spray more times than I want to — five applications at least, maybe six if I see them early. I use what the shop sells. I have no choice.

I do not test my soil. I apply fertilizer by the bag, roughly what I have always applied. More than the government says, probably, but I cannot afford a bad harvest.
